Correct Answer: C
Paragraph 22 opens with "That put the thing in a new light," the narrator's signal that Tom's question about whitewashing has changed Ben's view; right after it, Ben stops nibbling his apple and watches with growing interest. Choice A shows Ben mocking Tom before any change. Choice B shows Ben still doubting that anyone could like the work. Choice D shows the result of the change after it has already happened, not the moment it begins.

passage.html:
Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer"

Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. passage.html:
Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer"
by Mark Twain
1 But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.
2 He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:
3 “Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.
4 “Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.
5 “Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.
6 “Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.
7 “Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).
8 Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”
9 No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:
10 “Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”
11 Tom wheeled suddenly and said:
12 “Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”
13 “Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”
14 Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:
15 “What do you call work?”
16 “Why, ain’t that work?”
17 Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:
18 “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”
19 “Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”
20 The brush continued to move.
21 “Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:

24 Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:
25 “No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer"
by Mark Twain
1 But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.
2 He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:
3 “Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.
4 “Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.
5 “Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.
6 “Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.
7 “Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).
8 Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”
9 No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:
10 “Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”
11 Tom wheeled suddenly and said:
12 “Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”
13 “Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”
14 Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:
15 “What do you call work?”
16 “Why, ain’t that work?”
17 Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:
18 “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”
19 “Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”
20 The brush continued to move.
21 “Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”
22 That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:
23 “Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”
24 Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:
25 “No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”
26 “No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”
27 “Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”
28 “Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”
29 “Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”
30 “I’ll give you all of it!”
31 Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A
In paragraph 1 Tom considers paying the boys with his "worldly wealth" but gives up because it is not enough; in paragraph 31 the boys instead hand over a kite, a dead rat, and other goods to do the work, so the plan reverses the trade. Choice B is contradicted because Tom keeps his toys, choice C is unsupported because Aunt Polly never appears, and choice D is wrong because nothing in paragraph 31 shows the boys admiring Tom's skill.

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A
The narrator applies mock-heroic labels to a boyhood trade: Ben becomes "the late steamer Big Missouri," Tom becomes "the retired artist," and the boys he will trick are "innocents" facing "slaughter." Using such grand language for a prank creates amused irony, not condemnation. Choice B takes "slaughter" literally even though the boys trade happily. Choice C misreads "sweated" and "fagged," which are said in the same playful voice. Choice D mistakes a detail about how long the trading lasted for boredom.

passage.html:
Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer"
by Mark Twain
1 But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.
2 He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:
3 “Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.
4 “Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.
5 “Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.
6 “Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.
7 “Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).
8 Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”
9 No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:
10 “Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”
11 Tom wheeled suddenly and said:
12 “Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”
13 “Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”
14 Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:
15 “What do you call work?”
16 “Why, ain’t that work?”
17 Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:
18 “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”
19 “Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”
20 The brush continued to move.
21 “Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”
22 That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:
23 “Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”
24 Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:
25 “No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”
26 “No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”
27 “Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”
28 “Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”
29 “Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”
30 “I’ll give you all of it!”
31 Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B
Tom "paid no attention to the steamboat," surveys his brushwork "with the eye of an artist," and only notices Ben with a pretended start: "Why, it's you, Ben! I warn't noticing." This act makes Ben approach Tom and keeps Tom from seeming envious of Ben's freedom. Choice A mistakes the pretense for real enjoyment, which paragraph 31 contradicts. Choice C is wrong because Tom carries out the plan. Choice D invents earlier teasing the passage never describes.

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A
Whitewashing is the same chore from start to finish, but once Tom presents it as a rare privilege ("Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?"), Ben and the other boys pay to do it. Choice B is unsupported because the boys "remained to whitewash" and show no loss of trust. Choice C builds on Ben's serious game but adds a comparison with adult jobs that the passage never makes. Choice D is wrong because Ben is not careless; he recognizes the task as work in paragraph 16.

Mark Twain (1835–1910) was an American writer and humorist. The following is an excerpt from his 1876 novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer. In this scene, Tom, a boy in a small town on the Mississippi River, has been ordered to whitewash a long board fence on a Saturday morning.
Excerpt from "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer" by Mark Twain

But Tom’s energy did not last. He began to think of the fun he had planned for this day, and his sorrows multiplied. Soon the free boys would come tripping along on all sorts of delicious expeditions, and they would make a world of fun of him for having to work—the very thought of it burnt him like fire. He got out his worldly wealth and examined it—bits of toys, marbles, and trash; enough to buy an exchange of work, maybe, but not half enough to buy so much as half an hour of pure freedom. So he returned his straitened means to his pocket, and gave up the idea of trying to buy the boys. At this dark and hopeless moment an inspiration burst upon him! Nothing less than a great, magnificent inspiration.


He took up his brush and went tranquilly to work. Ben Rogers hove in sight presently—the very boy, of all boys, whose ridicule he had been dreading. Ben’s gait was the hop-skip-and-jump—proof enough that his heart was light and his anticipations high. He was eating an apple, and giving a long, melodious whoop, at intervals, followed by a deep-toned ding-dong-dong, ding-dong-dong, for he was personating a steamboat. As he drew near, he slackened speed, took the middle of the street, leaned far over to starboard and rounded to ponderously and with laborious pomp and circumstance—for he was personating the Big Missouri, and considered himself to be drawing nine feet of water. He was boat and captain and engine-bells combined, so he had to imagine himself standing on his own hurricane-deck giving the orders and executing them:


“Stop her, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling!” The headway ran almost out, and he drew up slowly toward the sidewalk.


“Ship up to back! Ting-a-ling-ling!” His arms straightened and stiffened down his sides.


“Set her back on the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow! ch-chow-wow! Chow!” His right hand, mean-time, describing stately circles—for it was representing a forty-foot wheel.


“Let her go back on the labboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ch-chow-chow!” The left hand began to describe circles.


“Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Come ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get out that head-line! lively now! Come—out with your spring-line—what’re you about there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight of it! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Done with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (trying the gauge-cocks).


Tom went on whitewashing—paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared a moment and then said: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a stump, ain’t you!”


No answer. Tom surveyed his last touch with the eye of an artist, then he gave his brush another gentle sweep and surveyed the result, as before. Ben ranged up alongside of him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stuck to his work. Ben said:


“Hello, old chap, you got to work, hey?”


Tom wheeled suddenly and said:


“Why, it’s you, Ben! I warn’t noticing.”


“Say—I’m going in a-swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d druther work—wouldn’t you? Course you would!”


Tom contemplated the boy a bit, and said:


“What do you call work?”


“Why, ain’t that work?”


Tom resumed his whitewashing, and answered carelessly:


“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t. All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”


“Oh come, now, you don’t mean to let on that you like it?”


The brush continued to move.


“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”


That put the thing in a new light. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom swept his brush daintily back and forth—stepped back to note the effect—added a touch here and there—criticised the effect again—Ben watching every move and getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Presently he said:


“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”


Tom considered, was about to consent; but he altered his mind:


“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s awful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I wouldn’t mind and she wouldn’t. Yes, she’s awful particular about this fence; it’s got to be done very careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, that can do it the way it’s got to be done.”


“No—is that so? Oh come, now—lemme just try. Only just a little—I’d let you, if you was me, Tom.”


“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid. Now don’t you see how I’m fixed? If you was to tackle this fence and anything was to happen to it—”


“Oh, shucks, I’ll be just as careful. Now lemme try. Say—I’ll give you the core of my apple.”


“Well, here—No, Ben, now don’t. I’m afeard—”


“I’ll give you all of it!”


Tom gave up the brush with reluctance in his face, but alacrity in his heart. And while the late steamer Big Missouri worked and sweated in the sun, the retired artist sat on a barrel in the shade close by, dangled his legs, munched his apple, and planned the slaughter of more innocents. There was no lack of material; boys happened along every little while; they came to jeer, but remained to whitewash. By the time Ben was fagged out, Tom had traded the next chance to Billy Fisher for a kite, in good repair; and when he played out, Johnny Miller bought in for a dead rat and a string to swing it with—and so on, and so on, hour after hour.

Correct Answer: D
"Seemed" signals that the $5,000 only appeared small. Paragraph 10 returns to the same contrast ("From a $5,000 purchase to a collection of more than 178 million items"), so the word sets up a tone of quiet admiration for the Library's growth. Choice A borrows the funding troubles of paragraph 2, but the author reports them without blaming Congress. Choice C misreads the setbacks as proof against the purchase, but the passage presents them as obstacles that the Library overcame. Choice B finds a mockery that the passage never expresses.

formattedBlocks.html: In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. In the more than two centuries since, that small shelf of books has grown into a collection of more than 178 million items.
formattedBlocks.text: In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. In the more than two centuries since, that small shelf of books has grown into a collection of more than 178 million items.

formattedBlocks.html: The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.
formattedBlocks.text: The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.

formattedBlocks.html: The worst setback came in 1814, when British troops burned Washington. The fire destroyed the Capitol and the small congressional library housed in its north wing. passage.html:
Adapted from "General Information" and "History of the Library," Library of Congress
From a Small Shelf to a Giant Collection: The Library of Congress

In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. In the more than two centuries since, that small shelf of books has grown into a collection of more than 178 million items.


The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.


The worst setback came in 1814, when British troops burned Washington. The fire destroyed the Capitol and the small congressional library housed in its north wing. Jefferson then offered to sell his personal library of 6,487 books to help Congress start over, and Congress accepted. Jefferson believed that a national library should gather knowledge on every subject. That idea, which he called universality, still shapes the Library's policy of collecting comprehensively.


After the Civil War, the Library began to take on its modern role. Ainsworth Rand Spofford, who served as Librarian from 1864 to 1897, promoted the Library as the nation's library rather than only a resource for lawmakers. A major step came in 1870, when Congress centralized copyright registration and deposit at the Library. The Library calls that change essential to the yearly growth of its collection. In 1897, the Library moved into its own building, the Thomas Jefferson Building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance style. When it opened, it was hailed as the largest, costliest, and safest library building in the world.


The twentieth century brought both new treasures and new duties. In 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt transferred the records of the Continental Congress and the personal papers of six founding fathers to the Library. During World War II, Librarian Archibald MacLeish helped send the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution to Fort Knox, Kentucky, and other safe sites. Growth continued in the decades that followed. Under Librarian L. Quincy Mumford, who served from 1954 to 1974, the book collection rose from 10 million to 17 million volumes. During the same period, the staff grew from 1,600 to 4,500 people, and the yearly appropriation rose from $9.5 million to $116 million.


Today, the Library's work takes place in several locations. Three buildings on Capitol Hill, named for Jefferson, John Adams, and James Madison, hold much of the collection. Other facilities extend that space. The High Density Storage Facility, which opened in 2002 at Fort Meade, Maryland, stores materials compactly. The Packard Campus for Audio Visual Conservation, which opened in 2007 in Culpeper, Virginia, cares for recordings and films.


The Library counted its holdings for fiscal year 2023, which ran from October 2022 to September 2023. That count lists more than 25.77 million cataloged books and a total of more than 178.2 million items. Beyond books, the Library holds enormous special collections of materials that are not books at all. Manuscripts form the largest group, at 78.5 million items. In fact, the manuscript collection is larger than the seven other types of material named in the next paragraph put together.


Those other groups show how varied the collections are. Microforms number 17.5 million, and photographs follow closely at 15.7 million. Sheet music totals 8.2 million items, and maps total 5.8 million. Audio materials number 4.3 million, machine-readable items such as computer files number 2 million, and moving images number 1.8 million. Other kinds of material, such as posters, prints, and drawings, are not counted here.


The Library's collections are also remarkably wide in language and reach. Its print materials alone are written in 470 languages. In fiscal year 2023, the Library answered more than 681,000 reference requests from Congress, the public, and other federal agencies. It also circulated more than 24.5 million copies of braille, audio, and large-print items. These items went to patrons who are blind or print disabled.


From a $5,000 purchase to a collection of more than 178 million items, the Library of Congress has traveled a long road. Fires, wars, and shortages of money and space slowed it at times, yet the collection kept growing. In that sense, Jefferson's idea of universality still guides the Library today. It collects knowledge in many forms, and it works to make that knowledge available to as many people as possible.

Adapted from "General Information" and "History of the Library," Library of Congress
From a Small Shelf to a Giant Collection: The Library of Congress
1 In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. 2 The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.
3 The worst setback came in 1814, when British troops burned Washington. The fire destroyed the Capitol and the small congressional library housed in its north wing. Jefferson then offered to sell his personal library of 6,487 books to help Congress start over, and Congress accepted. Jefferson believed that a national library should gather knowledge on every subject. That idea, which he called universality, still shapes the Library's policy of collecting comprehensively.
4 After the Civil War, the Library began to take on its modern role. Ainsworth Rand Spofford, who served as Librarian from 1864 to 1897, promoted the Library as the nation's library rather than only a resource for lawmakers. A major step came in 1870, when Congress centralized copyright registration and deposit at the Library. The Library calls that change essential to the yearly growth of its collection. In 1897, the Library moved into its own building, the Thomas Jefferson Building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance style. When it opened, it was hailed as the largest, costliest, and safest library building in the world.

In 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt transferred the records of the Continental Congress and the personal papers of six founding fathers to the Library. During World War II, Librarian Archibald MacLeish helped send the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution to Fort Knox, Kentucky, and other safe sites. Growth continued in the decades that followed. Under Librarian L. Quincy Mumford, who served from 1954 to 1974, the book collection rose from 10 million to 17 million volumes.
