passage.html:
Adapted from "General Information" and "History of the Library," Library of Congress
From a Small Shelf to a Giant Collection: The Library of Congress

In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. In the more than two centuries since, that small shelf of books has grown into a collection of more than 178 million items.


The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.


The worst setback came in 1814, when British troops burned Washington. The fire destroyed the Capitol and the small congressional library housed in its north wing. Jefferson then offered to sell his personal library of 6,487 books to help Congress start over, and Congress accepted. Jefferson believed that a national library should gather knowledge on every subject. That idea, which he called universality, still shapes the Library's policy of collecting comprehensively.


After the Civil War, the Library began to take on its modern role. Ainsworth Rand Spofford, who served as Librarian from 1864 to 1897, promoted the Library as the nation's library rather than only a resource for lawmakers. A major step came in 1870, when Congress centralized copyright registration and deposit at the Library. The Library calls that change essential to the yearly growth of its collection. In 1897, the Library moved into its own building, the Thomas Jefferson Building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance style. When it opened, it was hailed as the largest, costliest, and safest library building in the world.


The twentieth century brought both new treasures and new duties. In 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt transferred the records of the Continental Congress and the personal papers of six founding fathers to the Library. During World War II, Librarian Archibald MacLeish helped send the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution to Fort Knox, Kentucky, and other safe sites. Growth continued in the decades that followed. Under Librarian L. Quincy Mumford, who served from 1954 to 1974, the book collection rose from 10 million to 17 million volumes. During the same period, the staff grew from 1,600 to 4,500 people, and the yearly appropriation rose from $9.5 million to $116 million.


Today, the Library's work takes place in several locations. Three buildings on Capitol Hill, named for Jefferson, John Adams, and James Madison, hold much of the collection. Other facilities extend that space. The High Density Storage Facility, which opened in 2002 at Fort Meade, Maryland, stores materials compactly. The Packard Campus for Audio Visual Conservation, which opened in 2007 in Culpeper, Virginia, cares for recordings and films.


The Library counted its holdings for fiscal year 2023, which ran from October 2022 to September 2023. That count lists more than 25.77 million cataloged books and a total of more than 178.2 million items. Beyond books, the Library holds enormous special collections of materials that are not books at all. Manuscripts form the largest group, at 78.5 million items. In fact, the manuscript collection is larger than the seven other types of material named in the next paragraph put together.


Those other groups show how varied the collections are. Microforms number 17.5 million, and photographs follow closely at 15.7 million. Sheet music totals 8.2 million items, and maps total 5.8 million. Audio materials number 4.3 million, machine-readable items such as computer files number 2 million, and moving images number 1.8 million. Other kinds of material, such as posters, prints, and drawings, are not counted here.


The Library's collections are also remarkably wide in language and reach. Its print materials alone are written in 470 languages. In fiscal year 2023, the Library answered more than 681,000 reference requests from Congress, the public, and other federal agencies. It also circulated more than 24.5 million copies of braille, audio, and large-print items. These items went to patrons who are blind or print disabled.


From a $5,000 purchase to a collection of more than 178 million items, the Library of Congress has traveled a long road. Fires, wars, and shortages of money and space slowed it at times, yet the collection kept growing. In that sense, Jefferson's idea of universality still guides the Library today. It collects knowledge in many forms, and it works to make that knowledge available to as many people as possible.

Adapted from "General Information" and "History of the Library," Library of Congress

1 In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. In the more than two centuries since, that small shelf of books has grown into a collection of more than 178 million items.
2 The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.
3 The worst setback came in 1814, when British troops burned Washington. The fire destroyed the Capitol and the small congressional library housed in its north wing. Jefferson then offered to sell his personal library of 6,487 books to help Congress start over, and Congress accepted. Jefferson believed that a national library should gather knowledge on every subject. That idea, which he called universality, still shapes the Library's policy of collecting comprehensively.
4 After the Civil War, the Library began to take on its modern role. Ainsworth Rand Spofford, who served as Librarian from 1864 to 1897, promoted the Library as the nation's library rather than only a resource for lawmakers. A major step came in 1870, when Congress centralized copyright registration and deposit at the Library. The Library calls that change essential to the yearly growth of its collection. In 1897, the Library moved into its own building, the Thomas Jefferson Building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance style. When it opened, it was hailed as the largest, costliest, and safest library building in the world.
5 The twentieth century brought both new treasures and new duties. In 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt transferred the records of the Continental Congress and the personal papers of six founding fathers to the Library. During World War II, Librarian Archibald MacLeish helped send the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution to Fort Knox, Kentucky, and other safe sites. Growth continued in the decades that followed. Under Librarian L. Quincy Mumford, who served from 1954 to 1974, the book collection rose from 10 million to 17 million volumes. During the same period, the staff grew from 1,600 to 4,500 people, and the yearly appropriation rose from $9.5 million to $116 million.
6 Today, the Library's work takes place in several locations. Three buildings on Capitol Hill, named for Jefferson, John Adams, and James Madison, hold much of the collection. Other facilities extend that space. The High Density Storage Facility, which opened in 2002 at Fort Meade, Maryland, stores materials compactly. The Packard Campus for Audio Visual Conservation, which opened in 2007 in Culpeper, Virginia, cares for recordings and films.
7 The Library counted its holdings for fiscal year 2023, which ran from October 2022 to September 2023. That count lists more than 25.77 million cataloged books and a total of more than 178.2 million items. Beyond books, the Library holds enormous special collections of materials that are not books at all. Manuscripts form the largest group, at 78.5 million items. In fact, the manuscript collection is larger than the seven other types of material named in the next paragraph put together.

Sheet music totals 8.2 million items, and maps total 5.8 million. Audio materials number 4.3 million, machine-readable items such as computer files number 2 million, and moving images number 1.8 million. Other kinds of material, such as posters, prints, and drawings, are not counted here.

Adapted from "General Information" and "History of the Library," Library of Congress
From a Small Shelf to a Giant Collection: The Library of Congress

In 1800, President John Adams approved a law that gave Congress $5,000 to buy books. The sum seemed modest, yet that purchase marked the beginning of the Library of Congress. The first books were kept inside the U.S. Capitol, and a joint committee of Congress oversaw them. In the more than two centuries since, that small shelf of books has grown into a collection of more than 178 million items.


The early years were not easy. In 1802, President Thomas Jefferson approved a compromise that made the Librarian of Congress a position filled by the president. The first two Librarians each also served as clerk of the House of Representatives. For several decades, the Library mainly served Congress, and it often struggled with fires and a lack of space. It also had no yearly appropriation, so its leaders could never be sure how much money would be available to buy new books.


The worst setback came in 1814, when British troops burned Washington. The fire destroyed the Capitol and the small congressional library housed in its north wing. Jefferson then offered to sell his personal library of 6,487 books to help Congress start over, and Congress accepted. Jefferson believed that a national library should gather knowledge on every subject. That idea, which he called universality, still shapes the Library's policy of collecting comprehensively.


After the Civil War, the Library began to take on its modern role. Ainsworth Rand Spofford, who served as Librarian from 1864 to 1897, promoted the Library as the nation's library rather than only a resource for lawmakers. A major step came in 1870, when Congress centralized copyright registration and deposit at the Library. The Library calls that change essential to the yearly growth of its collection. In 1897, the Library moved into its own building, the Thomas Jefferson Building, which was designed in the Italian Renaissance style. When it opened, it was hailed as the largest, costliest, and safest library building in the world.


The twentieth century brought both new treasures and new duties. In 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt transferred the records of the Continental Congress and the personal papers of six founding fathers to the Library. During World War II, Librarian Archibald MacLeish helped send the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution to Fort Knox, Kentucky, and other safe sites. Growth continued in the decades that followed. Under Librarian L. Quincy Mumford, who served from 1954 to 1974, the book collection rose from 10 million to 17 million volumes. During the same period, the staff grew from 1,600 to 4,500 people, and the yearly appropriation rose from $9.5 million to $116 million.


Today, the Library's work takes place in several locations. Three buildings on Capitol Hill, named for Jefferson, John Adams, and James Madison, hold much of the collection. Other facilities extend that space. The High Density Storage Facility, which opened in 2002 at Fort Meade, Maryland, stores materials compactly. The Packard Campus for Audio Visual Conservation, which opened in 2007 in Culpeper, Virginia, cares for recordings and films.


The Library counted its holdings for fiscal year 2023, which ran from October 2022 to September 2023. That count lists more than 25.77 million cataloged books and a total of more than 178.2 million items. Beyond books, the Library holds enormous special collections of materials that are not books at all. Manuscripts form the largest group, at 78.5 million items. In fact, the manuscript collection is larger than the seven other types of material named in the next paragraph put together.


Those other groups show how varied the collections are. Microforms number 17.5 million, and photographs follow closely at 15.7 million. Sheet music totals 8.2 million items, and maps total 5.8 million. Audio materials number 4.3 million, machine-readable items such as computer files number 2 million, and moving images number 1.8 million. Other kinds of material, such as posters, prints, and drawings, are not counted here.


The Library's collections are also remarkably wide in language and reach. Its print materials alone are written in 470 languages. In fiscal year 2023, the Library answered more than 681,000 reference requests from Congress, the public, and other federal agencies. It also circulated more than 24.5 million copies of braille, audio, and large-print items. These items went to patrons who are blind or print disabled.


From a $5,000 purchase to a collection of more than 178 million items, the Library of Congress has traveled a long road. Fires, wars, and shortages of money and space slowed it at times, yet the collection kept growing. In that sense, Jefferson's idea of universality still guides the Library today. It collects knowledge in many forms, and it works to make that knowledge available to as many people as possible.

Where Jazz Began: The Music of Early New Orleans

In the early 1900s, the port city of New Orleans, Louisiana, gave rise to a new kind of music that blended many traditions into a sound no one had heard before. That sound came to be called jazz. Researchers who study its history disagree about exactly where and when it began, and no single person or date can claim the credit. Even so, the story of jazz is closely tied to New Orleans, a city whose mix of cultures made it an ideal place for musical invention.


The roots of that mix reach back to the city's founding. The French established New Orleans in 1718, and by 1721 enslaved West Africans made up about 30 percent of its population. By the middle of the 1700s, enslaved and free people of African descent were gathering in a place known as Congo Square. There they sang, danced, and played drums and other instruments, keeping alive rhythms and musical habits that came from West Africa. Those traditions did not vanish after slavery ended. Instead, they shaped the music of the city for generations.


By the 1880s, New Orleans had a lively street-music culture. Brass bands such as the Excelsior and the Onward played at parades, funerals, picnics, and dances. Neighborhood groups called social aid and pleasure clubs organized many of these events, and crowds of dancing followers trailed behind the band in what became known as the second line. Meanwhile, groups called Mardi Gras Indian gangs developed their own chants and drum rhythms for the city's carnival season. Later jazz stars, including Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton, remembered these groups as an influence on their own playing.


Another ingredient came from ragtime, a bouncy, syncopated style of piano music that grew popular by the 1890s. Around the same time, the city's Creole musicians of color, many of whom had formal training and could read written music, found their world changing. New segregation laws in the 1890s forced them to live and work alongside the uptown Black musicians, who often played by ear and loved to improvise. Neither group had all the skills of the other. Together, they produced a style that combined careful technique with free invention.


No figure is more closely linked with this early blending than the cornet player Charles "Buddy" Bolden. He formed a band in 1895 and gained a following by playing the blues and by speeding up the dance tunes of the day until they sounded lively and syncopated. His group performed at Funky Butt Hall and in Johnson Park and Lincoln Park. It also used the lineup that later became standard for New Orleans jazz, with a cornet, a clarinet, and a trombone out front. In 1906, Bolden collapsed during a parade. He was committed to a hospital in 1907, and his career was over. Still, other bands carried his methods forward.


One of those musicians was the trombonist Kid Ory, who was leading a band by 1901. After he moved to New Orleans in 1907, Ory played at Pete Lala's, a popular saloon in the Storyville district. In 1921, he became the first Black New Orleans jazz bandleader to make a record. Recordings mattered a great deal, because they allowed listeners far from the city to hear jazz for the first time.


In fact, jazz had already begun to travel. Morton toured outside Louisiana as early as 1907. In 1914, the Original Creole Orchestra reached California and then played the Orpheum circuit, a chain of major theaters across the country. A year later, Tom Brown's Band took the music to Chicago, and in 1916 and 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played in Chicago and New York. passage.html:
Adapted from "Early Jazz History" and "Jazz History," National Park Service
Where Jazz Began: The Music of Early New Orleans

In the early 1900s, the port city of New Orleans, Louisiana, gave rise to a new kind of music that blended many traditions into a sound no one had heard before. That sound came to be called jazz. Researchers who study its history disagree about exactly where and when it began, and no single person or date can claim the credit. Even so, the story of jazz is closely tied to New Orleans, a city whose mix of cultures made it an ideal place for musical invention.


The roots of that mix reach back to the city's founding. The French established New Orleans in 1718, and by 1721 enslaved West Africans made up about 30 percent of its population. By the middle of the 1700s, enslaved and free people of African descent were gathering in a place known as Congo Square. There they sang, danced, and played drums and other instruments, keeping alive rhythms and musical habits that came from West Africa. Those traditions did not vanish after slavery ended. Instead, they shaped the music of the city for generations.


By the 1880s, New Orleans had a lively street-music culture. Brass bands such as the Excelsior and the Onward played at parades, funerals, picnics, and dances. Neighborhood groups called social aid and pleasure clubs organized many of these events, and crowds of dancing followers trailed behind the band in what became known as the second line. Meanwhile, groups called Mardi Gras Indian gangs developed their own chants and drum rhythms for the city's carnival season. Later jazz stars, including Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton, remembered these groups as an influence on their own playing.


Another ingredient came from ragtime, a bouncy, syncopated style of piano music that grew popular by the 1890s. Around the same time, the city's Creole musicians of color, many of whom had formal training and could read written music, found their world changing. New segregation laws in the 1890s forced them to live and work alongside the uptown Black musicians, who often played by ear and loved to improvise. Neither group had all the skills of the other. Together, they produced a style that combined careful technique with free invention.


No figure is more closely linked with this early blending than the cornet player Charles "Buddy" Bolden. He formed a band in 1895 and gained a following by playing the blues and by speeding up the dance tunes of the day until they sounded lively and syncopated. His group performed at Funky Butt Hall and in Johnson Park and Lincoln Park. It also used the lineup that later became standard for New Orleans jazz, with a cornet, a clarinet, and a trombone out front. In 1906, Bolden collapsed during a parade. He was committed to a hospital in 1907, and his career was over. Still, other bands carried his methods forward.


One of those musicians was the trombonist Kid Ory, who was leading a band by 1901. After he moved to New Orleans in 1907, Ory played at Pete Lala's, a popular saloon in the Storyville district. In 1921, he became the first Black New Orleans jazz bandleader to make a record. Recordings mattered a great deal, because they allowed listeners far from the city to hear jazz for the first time.


In fact, jazz had already begun to travel. Morton toured outside Louisiana as early as 1907. In 1914, the Original Creole Orchestra reached California and then played the Orpheum circuit, a chain of major theaters across the country. A year later, Tom Brown's Band took the music to Chicago, and in 1916 and 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played in Chicago and New York. In February 1917, that group made "Livery Stable Blues," widely described as the first commercial jazz recording. It sold more than one million copies in six months. The timing was lucky, since record production in the United States had climbed from about 25 million records in 1914 to about 100 million in 1921.


Chicago soon became a second home for New Orleans musicians. Cornetist Joe "King" Oliver moved there in 1919, and in 1922 his Creole Jazz Band became the most admired group in the city. That summer, a young Louis Armstrong arrived from New Orleans to join it. In July 1923, a landmark session took place when the New Orleans Rhythm Kings recorded with Jelly Roll Morton. It was the first racially integrated jazz recording session, which was a bold step in an era of strict segregation.


Armstrong soon outgrew the band he had joined. From 1925 to 1928, he led the recording groups known as the Hot Five and the Hot Seven, whose records are still studied today. In February 1926, he recorded "Heebie Jeebies," in which he sang nonsense syllables in place of words. The style, called scat, spread quickly, and the same gift for invention could be heard in his trumpet solos. By the 1930s, jazz had grown into the swing era, when big bands filled dance halls across the nation.


The story of jazz, then, is not the story of one inventor or one night. It is the story of many people and traditions meeting in one crowded, musical city and then carrying their sound across the country. Today, the National Park Service helps preserve that history at New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park, where visitors can learn how the music began.

Where Jazz Began: The Music of Early New Orleans
1 In the early 1900s, the port city of New Orleans, Louisiana, gave rise to a new kind of music that blended many traditions into a sound no one had heard before. That sound came to be called jazz. Researchers who study its history disagree about exactly where and when it began, and no single person or date can claim the credit. Even so, the story of jazz is closely tied to New Orleans, a city whose mix of cultures made it an ideal place for musical invention.
2 The roots of that mix reach back to the city's founding. The French established New Orleans in 1718, and by 1721 enslaved West Africans made up about 30 percent of its population. By the middle of the 1700s, enslaved and free people of African descent were gathering in a place known as Congo Square. There they sang, danced, and played drums and other instruments, keeping alive rhythms and musical habits that came from West Africa. Those traditions did not vanish after slavery ended. Instead, they shaped the music of the city for generations.
3 By the 1880s, New Orleans had a lively street-music culture. Brass bands such as the Excelsior and the Onward played at parades, funerals, picnics, and dances. Neighborhood groups called social aid and pleasure clubs organized many of these events, and crowds of dancing followers trailed behind the band in what became known as the second line. Meanwhile, groups called Mardi Gras Indian gangs developed their own chants and drum rhythms for the city's carnival season. Later jazz stars, including Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton, remembered these groups as an influence on their own playing.
4 Another ingredient came from ragtime, a bouncy, syncopated style of piano music that grew popular by the 1890s. Around the same time, the city's Creole musicians of color, many of whom had formal training and could read written music, found their world changing. New segregation laws in the 1890s forced them to live and work alongside the uptown Black musicians, who often played by ear and loved to improvise. Neither group had all the skills of the other. Together, they produced a style that combined careful technique with free invention.
5 No figure is more closely linked with this early blending than the cornet player Charles "Buddy" Bolden. He formed a band in 1895 and gained a following by playing the blues and by speeding up the dance tunes of the day until they sounded lively and syncopated. His group performed at Funky Butt Hall and in Johnson Park and Lincoln Park. It also used the lineup that later became standard for New Orleans jazz, with a cornet, a clarinet, and a trombone out front. In 1906, Bolden collapsed during a parade. He was committed to a hospital in 1907, and his career was over. Still, other bands carried his methods forward.
6 One of those musicians was the trombonist Kid Ory, who was leading a band by 1901. After he moved to New Orleans in 1907, Ory played at Pete Lala's, a popular saloon in the Storyville district. In 1921, he became the first Black New Orleans jazz bandleader to make a record. Recordings mattered a great deal, because they allowed listeners far from the city to hear jazz for the first time.
7 In fact, jazz had already begun to travel. Morton toured outside Louisiana as early as 1907. In 1914, the Original Creole Orchestra reached California and then played the Orpheum circuit, a chain of major theaters across the country. A year later, Tom Brown's Band took the music to Chicago, and in 1916 and 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played in Chicago and New York. In February 1917, that group made "Livery Stable Blues," widely described as the first commercial jazz recording. It sold more than one million copies in six months. The timing was lucky, since record production in the United States had climbed from about 25 million records in 1914 to about 100 million in 1921.
8 Chicago soon became a second home for New Orleans musicians. Cornetist Joe "King" Oliver moved there in 1919, and in 1922 his Creole Jazz Band became the most admired group in the city. That summer, a young Louis Armstrong arrived from New Orleans to join it. In July 1923, a landmark session took place when the New Orleans Rhythm Kings recorded with Jelly Roll Morton. It was the first racially integrated jazz recording session, which was a bold step in an era of strict segregation.
9 Armstrong soon outgrew the band he had joined. From 1925 to 1928, he led the recording groups known as the Hot Five and the Hot Seven, whose records are still studied today. In February 1926, he recorded "Heebie Jeebies," in which he sang nonsense syllables in place of words. The style, called scat, spread quickly, and the same gift for invention could be heard in his trumpet solos. By the 1930s, jazz had grown into the swing era, when big bands filled dance halls across the nation.
10 The story of jazz, then, is not the story of one inventor or one night. It is the story of many people and traditions meeting in one crowded, musical city and then carrying their sound across the country. Today, the National Park Service helps preserve that history at New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park, where visitors can learn how the music began.

Where Jazz Began: The Music of Early New Orleans

In the early 1900s, the port city of New Orleans, Louisiana, gave rise to a new kind of music that blended many traditions into a sound no one had heard before. That sound came to be called jazz. Researchers who study its history disagree about exactly where and when it began, and no single person or date can claim the credit. Even so, the story of jazz is closely tied to New Orleans, a city whose mix of cultures made it an ideal place for musical invention.


The roots of that mix reach back to the city's founding. The French established New Orleans in 1718, and by 1721 enslaved West Africans made up about 30 percent of its population. By the middle of the 1700s, enslaved and free people of African descent were gathering in a place known as Congo Square. There they sang, danced, and played drums and other instruments, keeping alive rhythms and musical habits that came from West Africa. Those traditions did not vanish after slavery ended. Instead, they shaped the music of the city for generations.


By the 1880s, New Orleans had a lively street-music culture. Brass bands such as the Excelsior and the Onward played at parades, funerals, picnics, and dances. Neighborhood groups called social aid and pleasure clubs organized many of these events, and crowds of dancing followers trailed behind the band in what became known as the second line. Meanwhile, groups called Mardi Gras Indian gangs developed their own chants and drum rhythms for the city's carnival season. Later jazz stars, including Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton, remembered these groups as an influence on their own playing.


Another ingredient came from ragtime, a bouncy, syncopated style of piano music that grew popular by the 1890s. Around the same time, the city's Creole musicians of color, many of whom had formal training and could read written music, found their world changing. New segregation laws in the 1890s forced them to live and work alongside the uptown Black musicians, who often played by ear and loved to improvise. Neither group had all the skills of the other. Together, they produced a style that combined careful technique with free invention.


No figure is more closely linked with this early blending than the cornet player Charles "Buddy" Bolden. He formed a band in 1895 and gained a following by playing the blues and by speeding up the dance tunes of the day until they sounded lively and syncopated. His group performed at Funky Butt Hall and in Johnson Park and Lincoln Park. It also used the lineup that later became standard for New Orleans jazz, with a cornet, a clarinet, and a trombone out front. In 1906, Bolden collapsed during a parade. He was committed to a hospital in 1907, and his career was over. Still, other bands carried his methods forward.


One of those musicians was the trombonist Kid Ory, who was leading a band by 1901. After he moved to New Orleans in 1907, Ory played at Pete Lala's, a popular saloon in the Storyville district. In 1921, he became the first Black New Orleans jazz bandleader to make a record. Recordings mattered a great deal, because they allowed listeners far from the city to hear jazz for the first time.


In fact, jazz had already begun to travel. Morton toured outside Louisiana as early as 1907. In 1914, the Original Creole Orchestra reached California and then played the Orpheum circuit, a chain of major theaters across the country. A year later, Tom Brown's Band took the music to Chicago, and in 1916 and 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played in Chicago and New York. In February 1917, that group made "Livery Stable Blues," widely described as the first commercial jazz recording. It sold more than one million copies in six months. The timing was lucky, since record production in the United States had climbed from about 25 million records in 1914 to about 100 million in 1921.


Chicago soon became a second home for New Orleans musicians. Cornetist Joe "King" Oliver moved there in 1919, and in 1922 his Creole Jazz Band became the most admired group in the city. That summer, a young Louis Armstrong arrived from New Orleans to join it. In July 1923, a landmark session took place when the New Orleans Rhythm Kings recorded with Jelly Roll Morton. It was the first racially integrated jazz recording session, which was a bold step in an era of strict segregation.


Armstrong soon outgrew the band he had joined. From 1925 to 1928, he led the recording groups known as the Hot Five and the Hot Seven, whose records are still studied today. In February 1926, he recorded "Heebie Jeebies," in which he sang nonsense syllables in place of words. The style, called scat, spread quickly, and the same gift for invention could be heard in his trumpet solos. By the 1930s, jazz had grown into the swing era, when big bands filled dance halls across the nation.


The story of jazz, then, is not the story of one inventor or one night. It is the story of many people and traditions meeting in one crowded, musical city and then carrying their sound across the country. Today, the National Park Service helps preserve that history at New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park, where visitors can learn how the music began.

He was committed to a hospital in 1907, and his career was over. Still, other bands carried his methods forward.
6 One of those musicians was the trombonist Kid Ory, who was leading a band by 1901. After he moved to New Orleans in 1907, Ory played at Pete Lala's, a popular saloon in the Storyville district. In 1921, he became the first Black New Orleans jazz bandleader to make a record. Recordings mattered a great deal, because they allowed listeners far from the city to hear jazz for the first time.
7 In fact, jazz had already begun to travel. Morton toured outside Louisiana as early as 1907. In 1914, the Original Creole Orchestra reached California and then played the Orpheum circuit, a chain of major theaters across the country. A year later, Tom Brown's Band took the music to Chicago, and in 1916 and 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played in Chicago and New York. That summer, a young Louis Armstrong arrived from New Orleans to join it. In July 1923, a landmark session took place when the New Orleans Rhythm Kings recorded with Jelly Roll Morton. It was the first racially integrated jazz recording session, which was a bold step in an era of strict segregation.

In February 1926, he recorded "Heebie Jeebies," in which he sang nonsense syllables in place of words. By the 1930s, jazz had grown into the swing era, when big bands filled dance halls across the nation.

It is the story of many people and traditions meeting in one crowded, musical city and then carrying their sound across the country. Where Jazz Began: The Music of Early New Orleans

In the early 1900s, the port city of New Orleans, Louisiana, gave rise to a new kind of music that blended many traditions into a sound no one had heard before. That sound came to be called jazz. Researchers who study its history disagree about exactly where and when it began, and no single person or date can claim the credit. Even so, the story of jazz is closely tied to New Orleans, a city whose mix of cultures made it an ideal place for musical invention.


The roots of that mix reach back to the city's founding. The French established New Orleans in 1718, and by 1721 enslaved West Africans made up about 30 percent of its population. By the middle of the 1700s, enslaved and free people of African descent were gathering in a place known as Congo Square. There they sang, danced, and played drums and other instruments, keeping alive rhythms and musical habits that came from West Africa. Those traditions did not vanish after slavery ended. Instead, they shaped the music of the city for generations.


By the 1880s, New Orleans had a lively street-music culture. Brass bands such as the Excelsior and the Onward played at parades, funerals, picnics, and dances. Neighborhood groups called social aid and pleasure clubs organized many of these events, and crowds of dancing followers trailed behind the band in what became known as the second line. Meanwhile, groups called Mardi Gras Indian gangs developed their own chants and drum rhythms for the city's carnival season. Later jazz stars, including Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton, remembered these groups as an influence on their own playing.


Another ingredient came from ragtime, a bouncy, syncopated style of piano music that grew popular by the 1890s. Around the same time, the city's Creole musicians of color, many of whom had formal training and could read written music, found their world changing. New segregation laws in the 1890s forced them to live and work alongside the uptown Black musicians, who often played by ear and loved to improvise. Neither group had all the skills of the other. Together, they produced a style that combined careful technique with free invention.


No figure is more closely linked with this early blending than the cornet player Charles "Buddy" Bolden. He formed a band in 1895 and gained a following by playing the blues and by speeding up the dance tunes of the day until they sounded lively and syncopated. His group performed at Funky Butt Hall and in Johnson Park and Lincoln Park. It also used the lineup that later became standard for New Orleans jazz, with a cornet, a clarinet, and a trombone out front. In 1906, Bolden collapsed during a parade. He was committed to a hospital in 1907, and his career was over. Still, other bands carried his methods forward.


One of those musicians was the trombonist Kid Ory, who was leading a band by 1901. After he moved to New Orleans in 1907, Ory played at Pete Lala's, a popular saloon in the Storyville district. In 1921, he became the first Black New Orleans jazz bandleader to make a record. Recordings mattered a great deal, because they allowed listeners far from the city to hear jazz for the first time.


In fact, jazz had already begun to travel. Morton toured outside Louisiana as early as 1907. In 1914, the Original Creole Orchestra reached California and then played the Orpheum circuit, a chain of major theaters across the country. A year later, Tom Brown's Band took the music to Chicago, and in 1916 and 1917 the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played in Chicago and New York. In February 1917, that group made "Livery Stable Blues," widely described as the first commercial jazz recording. It sold more than one million copies in six months. The timing was lucky, since record production in the United States had climbed from about 25 million records in 1914 to about 100 million in 1921.


Chicago soon became a second home for New Orleans musicians. Cornetist Joe "King" Oliver moved there in 1919, and in 1922 his Creole Jazz Band became the most admired group in the city. That summer, a young Louis Armstrong arrived from New Orleans to join it. In July 1923, a landmark session took place when the New Orleans Rhythm Kings recorded with Jelly Roll Morton. It was the first racially integrated jazz recording session, which was a bold step in an era of strict segregation.


Armstrong soon outgrew the band he had joined. From 1925 to 1928, he led the recording groups known as the Hot Five and the Hot Seven, whose records are still studied today. In February 1926, he recorded "Heebie Jeebies," in which he sang nonsense syllables in place of words. The style, called scat, spread quickly, and the same gift for invention could be heard in his trumpet solos. By the 1930s, jazz had grown into the swing era, when big bands filled dance halls across the nation.


The story of jazz, then, is not the story of one inventor or one night. It is the story of many people and traditions meeting in one crowded, musical city and then carrying their sound across the country. Today, the National Park Service helps preserve that history at New Orleans Jazz National Historical Park, where visitors can learn how the music began.

passage.html:
Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who wrote nearly 1,800 poems, most of which were published after her death.

"A Bird came down the Walk"

by Emily Dickinson

A Bird came down the Walk—

He did not know I saw—

He bit an Angleworm in halves

And ate the fellow, raw,


And then he drank a Dew

From a convenient Grass—

And then hopped sidewise to the Wall

To let a Beetle pass—


He glanced with rapid eyes,

That hurried all around—

They looked like frightened Beads, I thought—

He stirred his Velvet Head


Like one in danger, Cautious,

I offered him a Crumb

And he unrolled his feathers,

And rowed him softer Home—


Than Oars divide the Ocean,

Too silver for a seam—

Or Butterflies, off Banks of Noon

Leap, plashless as they swim.

"A Bird came down the Walk"
by Emily Dickinson
A Bird came down the Walk—
He did not know I saw—
He bit an Angleworm in halves
And ate the fellow, raw,

And then he drank a Dew
From a convenient Grass—
And then hopped sidewise to the Wall
To let a Beetle pass—

He glanced with rapid eyes,
That hurried all around—
They looked like frightened Beads, I thought—
He stirred his Velvet Head

Like one in danger, Cautious,
I offered him a Crumb
And he unrolled his feathers,
And rowed him softer Home—

Than Oars divide the Ocean,
Too silver for a seam—
Or Butterflies, off Banks of Noon
Leap, plashless as they swim.

questions.explanation:

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: Plain words like "bit" and "raw," mixed with playful touches like "the fellow" and "a convenient Grass," create a calm, wryly amused tone.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B
Lines 3–6 report the meal plainly ("bit," "raw"), but calling the worm "the fellow" and the grass "convenient" adds dry humor, so the tone is calm and amused. Choice A ignores the humor and the later shift to wonder. Choice C misreads playful word choices as scientific ones. Choice D is wrong because the plain words state the violence openly rather than hiding it.

correctAnswer.label: C
correctAnswer.text: It lets the line describe both the wary bird and the careful speaker, linking the two at the moment the speaker reaches out.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C
The phrase can complete the third stanza's picture of the bird ("He stirred his Velvet Head / Like one in danger") or describe the speaker ("Cautious, / I offered him a Crumb"); the stanza break leaves both readings open, joining watcher and watched at the point of contact. Choice A adds a fear of attack the poem never suggests. Choice B is wrong because the line connects the two rather than separating them. Choice D invents a predator.

passage.html:
Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who wrote nearly 1,800 poems, most of which were published after her death.

"A Bird came down the Walk"

by Emily Dickinson

A Bird came down the Walk—

He did not know I saw—

He bit an Angleworm in halves

And ate the fellow, raw,


And then he drank a Dew

From a convenient Grass—

And then hopped sidewise to the Wall

To let a Beetle pass—


He glanced with rapid eyes,

That hurried all around—

They looked like frightened Beads, I thought—

He stirred his Velvet Head


Like one in danger, Cautious,

I offered him a Crumb

And he unrolled his feathers,

And rowed him softer Home—


Than Oars divide the Ocean,

Too silver for a seam—

Or Butterflies, off Banks of Noon

Leap, plashless as they swim.

Excerpt from "The Huddle and the Cold" by Margot Pelling

Antarctica in the depths of winter is a place that seems designed to end life rather than sustain it. The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Scientists who study polar biology often describe the emperor penguin as a particularly clear example of how multiple layers of adaptation can solve a problem that appears, at first glance, to be entirely unsolvable.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: C
Paragraph 4 calls the huddle a self-regulating system that drifts as a whole yet is 'not organized by any single leader' and 'emerges from individual responses,' which is why paragraph 1 says the group functions 'almost' like one organism. A is contradicted by paragraph 3's cycling, which keeps any bird from staying too long in the cold; B is contradicted by the absence of a leader; D is contradicted by paragraph 3, where core birds overheat and must move outward.

formattedBlocks.html: Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.

formattedBlocks.html: What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.

formattedBlocks.html: While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.

The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.

passage.html:
Margot Pelling is a science writer whose work appears in natural-history publications for general audiences. The following is adapted from her essay in Polar Margins Quarterly.
Excerpt from "The Huddle and the Cold" by Margot Pelling

Antarctica in the depths of winter is a place that seems designed to end life rather than sustain it. The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Scientists who study polar biology often describe the emperor penguin as a particularly clear example of how multiple layers of adaptation can solve a problem that appears, at first glance, to be entirely unsolvable.

Margot Pelling is a science writer whose work appears in natural-history publications for general audiences. The following is adapted from her essay in Polar Margins Quarterly.
Excerpt from "The Huddle and the Cold" by Margot Pelling

Antarctica in the depths of winter is a place that seems designed to end life rather than sustain it. The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Scientists who study polar biology often describe the emperor penguin as a particularly clear example of how multiple layers of adaptation can solve a problem that appears, at first glance, to be entirely unsolvable.

The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.
4 What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.
5 While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.
6 The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.
7 The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.
8 Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.
9 What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Scientists who study polar biology often describe the emperor penguin as a particularly clear example of how multiple layers of adaptation can solve a problem that appears, at first glance, to be entirely unsolvable.
