Antarctica in the depths of winter is a place that seems designed to end life rather than sustain it. The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Margot Pelling is a science writer whose work appears in natural-history publications for general audiences. The following is adapted from her essay in Polar Margins Quarterly.
Excerpt from "The Huddle and the Cold" by Margot Pelling

Antarctica in the depths of winter is a place that seems designed to end life rather than sustain it. The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Scientists who study polar biology often describe the emperor penguin as a particularly clear example of how multiple layers of adaptation can solve a problem that appears, at first glance, to be entirely unsolvable.

passage.html:
Margot Pelling is a science writer whose work appears in natural-history publications for general audiences. The following is adapted from her essay in Polar Margins Quarterly.
Excerpt from "The Huddle and the Cold" by Margot Pelling

Antarctica in the depths of winter is a place that seems designed to end life rather than sustain it. The sun disappears for weeks, winds scour the ice at speeds that can knock a person flat, and temperatures drop to levels that would freeze exposed skin in minutes. Yet in this environment, emperor penguins not only survive but also raise the next generation of chicks. Understanding how they manage this feat requires looking at behavior, physiology, and the unexpected ways a group of animals can function almost like a single organism.


Emperor penguins are the largest of all penguin species, and their size is one of their first defenses against the cold. A larger body holds more heat relative to the surface area that loses it. But size alone would not be enough. Beneath the skin, emperor penguins carry a thick layer of fat that acts as insulation, slowing the rate at which warmth escapes into the frigid air. Unlike most birds, they also have four overlapping layers of short, densely packed feathers that trap a film of still air next to the skin. That trapped air is an effective barrier, much the way a down jacket works by holding warmth close to the body rather than letting it circulate away.


Feathers and fat take a penguin only so far, however. The real marvel of winter survival for emperor penguins is a behavior called huddling. When temperatures fall and winds pick up, hundreds or even thousands of penguins press together in a dense cluster, forming what researchers sometimes call a huddle or a turtle formation. The birds on the outer edge of the huddle face inward, shielding those at the center while slowly cycling through the formation so that no individual spends too long in the coldest position. The result is that the average temperature inside a large huddle is dramatically warmer than the surrounding air — warm enough, in some documented cases, that the penguins at the core must periodically move to the outside to avoid overheating.


What makes the huddle so effective is collective heat production. Each penguin generates warmth through its own metabolism, and when thousands of bodies are pressed together, that warmth accumulates. Researchers who have studied huddle dynamics describe the cluster as a slow-moving, self-regulating system: as birds on the cold edge move inward and warm birds cycle outward, the entire formation drifts gradually across the ice over the course of hours. The movement is not random. It follows a pattern driven by the penguin's natural tendency to move toward warmth while the outer birds lean inward against the wind. The huddle is not organized by any single leader; it emerges from individual responses to temperature and crowding.


While the female emperor penguin feeds at sea during the Antarctic winter, the male is responsible for incubating the single egg the pair has produced. He balances the egg on the tops of his feet and draws a fold of warm belly skin, called a brood pouch, down over it. This keeps the egg several degrees warmer than the surrounding air. The male does not eat for the entire incubation period, which lasts roughly two months. He relies instead on the fat reserves he built up before winter began. By the time the egg hatches, a male emperor penguin may have lost a large share of his body weight. Figure 1 shows the approximate mass of one male as the fast goes on. The huddle allows him to spend far less energy fighting the cold, which means his fat reserves last long enough for the chick to hatch safely.


The timing of emperor penguin reproduction may seem counterintuitive — why breed in the worst possible season rather than the warmer months? The answer lies in the chick's development. By the time the egg hatches and the chick grows large enough to survive independently, it will be summer on the Antarctic coast, and the sea will be close, full of fish and squid. If the penguins waited for warmer weather to begin breeding, the chick would not be ready to feed at sea until the following winter. The harsh breeding season is, in a sense, a calculated trade-off that gives the chick the best possible start in the most productive season.


The female returns from the sea right around the time the egg hatches, carrying a stomach full of partially digested food she regurgitates to feed the newborn chick. The male, by this point lean and depleted, makes his way to the sea for his first meal in two months. The transition is precise: the chick is too fragile to survive without food for long, and the female's return is timed, through what scientists believe is a combination of internal biological rhythms and environmental cues, to match the hatching almost exactly. If she is delayed and the male's energy runs out before she arrives, the male may abandon the chick to feed, and the chick will not survive. The system works because it usually works — but it leaves little margin for error.


Emperor penguin chicks grow rapidly through the spring, sheltered in huddles of their own. Juvenile penguins cluster together in groups called crèches while both parents make trips to and from the sea. By midsummer the chicks have replaced their gray downy feathers with the waterproof adult plumage they need to enter the ocean. At that point the young penguins are on their own, and they find their way to the water with no guidance from their parents. The instinct to do so appears to be innate, emerging without being taught.


What makes the emperor penguin's story remarkable is that none of its individual adaptations — the fat, the feathers, the huddling, the timing of the breeding cycle — would be sufficient in isolation. It is the combination of all of them, working together across months of unrelenting cold, that allows the species to occupy a niche that no other bird on earth has claimed. Scientists who study polar biology often describe the emperor penguin as a particularly clear example of how multiple layers of adaptation can solve a problem that appears, at first glance, to be entirely unsolvable.

passage.html:
Langston Hughes (1901–1967) was an American poet and a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. "The Weary Blues" won first prize in the 1925 poetry contest of the magazine Opportunity and appeared in his 1926 collection The Weary Blues.

"The Weary Blues"

by Langston Hughes

Droning a drowsy syncopated tune,

Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon,

I heard a Negro play.

Down on Lenox Avenue the other night

By the pale dull pallor of an old gas light

He did a lazy sway. . . .

He did a lazy sway. . . .

To the tune o’ those Weary Blues.


With his ebony hands on each ivory key

He made that poor piano moan with melody.

O Blues!

Swaying to and fro on his rickety stool

He played that sad raggy tune like a musical fool.

Sweet Blues!

Coming from a black man’s soul.

O Blues!


In a deep song voice with a melancholy tone

I heard that Negro sing, that old piano moan—

“Ain’t got nobody in all this world,

Ain’t got nobody but ma self.

I’s gwine to quit ma frownin’

And put ma troubles on the shelf.”


Thump, thump, thump, went his foot on the floor.

He played a few chords then he sang some more—

“I got the Weary Blues

And I can’t be satisfied.

Got the Weary Blues

And can’t be satisfied—

I ain’t happy no mo’

And I wish that I had died.”


And far into the night he crooned that tune.

The stars went out and so did the moon.

The singer stopped playing and went to bed

While the Weary Blues echoed through his head.

He slept like a rock or a man that’s dead.

passage.html:
Langston Hughes (1901–1967) was an American poet and a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. "The Weary Blues" won first prize in the 1925 poetry contest of the magazine Opportunity and appeared in his 1926 collection The Weary Blues.

"The Weary Blues"

by Langston Hughes

Droning a drowsy syncopated tune,

Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon,

I heard a Negro play.

Down on Lenox Avenue the other night

By the pale dull pallor of an old gas light

He did a lazy sway. . . .

He did a lazy sway. . . .

To the tune o’ those Weary Blues.


With his ebony hands on each ivory key

He made that poor piano moan with melody.

O Blues!

Swaying to and fro on his rickety stool

He played that sad raggy tune like a musical fool.

Sweet Blues!

Coming from a black man’s soul.

O Blues!


In a deep song voice with a melancholy tone

I heard that Negro sing, that old piano moan—

“Ain’t got nobody in all this world,

Ain’t got nobody but ma self.

I’s gwine to quit ma frownin’

And put ma troubles on the shelf.”


Thump, thump, thump, went his foot on the floor.

He played a few chords then he sang some more—

“I got the Weary Blues

And I can’t be satisfied.

Got the Weary Blues

And can’t be satisfied—

I ain’t happy no mo’

And I wish that I had died.”


And far into the night he crooned that tune.

The stars went out and so did the moon.

The singer stopped playing and went to bed

While the Weary Blues echoed through his head.

He slept like a rock or a man that’s dead.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: A
The musician pours his sorrow into the blues throughout the night, yet he ends the poem sleeping "like a rock or a man that's dead" with the Weary Blues still echoing through his head, so the music expresses his pain without curing it. Choice B is contradicted by that ending. Choice C is unsupported, since the night brings no relief. Choice D is unsupported because the poem never describes an audience.

passage.html:
Langston Hughes (1901–1967) was an American poet and a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. "The Weary Blues" won first prize in the 1925 poetry contest of the magazine Opportunity and appeared in his 1926 collection The Weary Blues.

"The Weary Blues"

by Langston Hughes

Droning a drowsy syncopated tune,

Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon,

I heard a Negro play.

Down on Lenox Avenue the other night

By the pale dull pallor of an old gas light

He did a lazy sway. . . .

He did a lazy sway. . . .

To the tune o’ those Weary Blues.


With his ebony hands on each ivory key

He made that poor piano moan with melody.

O Blues!

Swaying to and fro on his rickety stool

He played that sad raggy tune like a musical fool.

Sweet Blues!

Coming from a black man’s soul.

O Blues!


In a deep song voice with a melancholy tone

I heard that Negro sing, that old piano moan—

“Ain’t got nobody in all this world,

Ain’t got nobody but ma self.

I’s gwine to quit ma frownin’

And put ma troubles on the shelf.”


Thump, thump, thump, went his foot on the floor.

He played a few chords then he sang some more—

“I got the Weary Blues

And I can’t be satisfied.

Got the Weary Blues

And can’t be satisfied—

I ain’t happy no mo’

And I wish that I had died.”


And far into the night he crooned that tune.

The stars went out and so did the moon.

The singer stopped playing and went to bed

While the Weary Blues echoed through his head.

He slept like a rock or a man that’s dead.

formattedBlocks.html: (1) Building a kite from scratch looks simple until you actually try it. (2) The frame has to be light but stiff, the sail has to catch wind without tearing, and the bridle has to hold every part in exactly the right position. (3) Most beginners discover these demands the hard way, watching their first attempt spin straight into the ground about ten seconds after launch. (4) Learning to make a good kite, it turns out, is mostly a matter of understanding why each piece matters.
formattedBlocks.text: (1) Building a kite from scratch looks simple until you actually try it. (2) The frame has to be light but stiff, the sail has to catch wind without tearing, and the bridle has to hold every part in exactly the right position. (3) Most beginners discover these demands the hard way, watching their first attempt spin straight into the ground about ten seconds after launch. (4) Learning to make a good kite, it turns out, is mostly a matter of understanding why each piece matters.

formattedBlocks.html: (5) The frame is the place to start. (6) Bamboo skewers work well for small kites because they bend slightly under pressure instead of snapping. (7) A kite maker lays two skewers in a cross, ties them at the intersection with waxed thread, and then runs a border string around the outside tips to create the kite's outline. (8) Once the frame is finished, the builder traces it onto a sheet of ripstop nylon and cuts the sail material about two centimeters beyond the frame on every side. (9) That extra margin gets folded over the border string and glued down, sealing the edge so the wind has nothing loose to grab. (10) Without that folded hem, a strong gust will peel the sail away from the frame in seconds, the sail can rip completely free before the kite even reaches full height. (11) A kite maker should test the frame on the ground before attaching the sail, pressing gently on both ends of the spine to check whether the bow is even.

formattedBlocks.html: (12) The bridle is where most beginners go wrong, and it is also the part that most directly controls how well a kite flies. (13) A standard delta kite uses a three-leg bridle: one line runs from the nose, and one line runs from each lower wing tip, and all three meet at a single tow point. (14) The tow point is where the flying line attaches, so its position determines the angle the kite holds against the wind. (15) Moving the tow point forward makes the kite climb steeply but lose stability; moving it back flattens the angle and steadies the flight. (16) When a builder adjusts the tow point, they should record the change so it can return the setting to its original position if the new angle performs worse. (17) A common beginner mistake is tying the bridle lines unequal in length, which causes the kite to pull hard to one side and spiral.

The passage's logic is a chain: the tail creates drag, and drag in turn slows spinning and keeps the nose up, so the appositive "the force that" keeps drag as the cause of both effects. (3) Most beginners discover these demands the hard way, watching their first attempt spin straight into the ground about ten seconds after launch. (4) Learning to make a good kite, it turns out, is mostly a matter of understanding why each piece matters.
(5) The frame is the place to start. (6) Bamboo skewers work well for small kites because they bend slightly under pressure instead of snapping. (7) A kite maker lays two skewers in a cross, ties them at the intersection with waxed thread, and then runs a border string around the outside tips to create the kite's outline. (8) Once the frame is finished, the builder traces it onto a sheet of ripstop nylon and cuts the sail material about two centimeters beyond the frame on every side. (9) That extra margin gets folded over the border string and glued down, sealing the edge so the wind has nothing loose to grab. (10) Without that folded hem, a strong gust will peel the sail away from the frame in seconds, the sail can rip completely free before the kite even reaches full height.
